analysis.one_liner: Writes the ban on trading stocks with inside information directly into federal law.
analysis.headline: The Senate bill was referred to the Banking Committee on August 6, 2026, and has seen no committee vote or floor action since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add a new section to the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 making it a direct violation of federal law to buy or sell securities while knowingly using material, nonpublic information — information obtained wrongfully, through theft, espionage, misappropriation, or a breach of duty to shareholders [S2]. Today that ban rests mostly on SEC rules and court interpretations; this would write it into statute and extend the SEC's enforcement tools to cover it [S2]. It applies to anyone who trades on inside information, which includes corporate executives, fund managers, and government officials [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary investors who trade without inside knowledge, because markets would have clearer, statute-backed rules against insiders profiting off information they should not have.

how_it_helps.text: Makes insider trading an explicit statutory violation of the Securities Exchange Act rather than relying on SEC rules and evolving court interpretations, giving regulators and prosecutors a firmer basis to act [S2].

Extends the SEC's enforcement authority — including treble-damages penalties under section 21A — to cover the new prohibition, so insider-trading enforcement would carry the same penalties as other securities fraud [S2].
The ban applies to any person, not just corporate insiders, so government officials and members of Congress trading on confidential information would fall squarely within it [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Insiders who currently trade on material nonpublic information — corporate executives, traders at funds with information advantages, and officials with confidential knowledge — who would face clear legal liability and treble damages.
analysis.who_pays_short: Insiders who trade on confidential information

drawbacks.text: The bill defines wrongful trading by a list of sources — theft, bribery, misappropriation, breach of fiduciary duty — and some securities-law scholars have argued any statutory codification risks freezing or loosening standards that courts and the SEC currently apply flexibly through Rule 10b5-1 case law [S2].

The bill preserves Rule 10b5-1 compliant transactions and lets the SEC exempt classes of traders by rule, so a reader should not assume it would close every avenue insiders currently use, including scheduled pre-planned trades [S2].

Codifying the ban could add compliance burden and potentially chill the lawful flow of market information to analysts and journalists, a standard concern with any insider-trading definition that sweeps broadly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a codification of an existing prohibition, so its practical day-to-day effect may be modest — insider trading is already illegal under SEC rules and case law. Its real value is durability: putting the ban in statute makes it harder to erode through litigation or regulatory drift, and it gives the SEC explicit statutory footing for enforcement and treble-damage actions. The main risk is drafting: a statutory definition that misses or mishandles the current standard could leave gaps that aggressive traders exploit.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee on August 6, 2026, and has sat there without a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Senator Jack Reed introduced the bill on August 6, 2026, joined by four Democratic cosponsors: Senators Van Hollen, Kim, Alsobrooks, and Blunt Rochester [S2][S3].
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs [S1][S4].
No further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — appears in the record since the referral [S4].
The Congress ends January 3, 2027, leaving a short window in which the bill has received no committee attention.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained and no one has lost; the bill simply sits unacted on in committee. If it dies there, insiders who trade on material nonpublic information are better off, since the existing rules-based framework stays in place rather than gaining statutory force.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody yet; the bill sits untouched in committee

for.name: Sen. Jack Reed
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Sens. Chris Van Hollen, Andy Kim, Lisa Blunt Rochester, and Angela Alsobrooks
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only four cosponsors at introduction.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors are Democrats and no Republicans cosponsored; there has been no vote, so no one has had to take a position on the record.

industries.industry: Insiders who trade on material nonpublic information (corporate executives, fund traders, officials with confidential knowledge)
industries.note: The bill makes their trading an explicit statutory violation with SEC treble-damages enforcement. Ordinary investors benefit from markets where they are not systematically trading against informed counterparties.

Firms would face a clearer statutory standard rather than shifting case law, which could aid compliance, but the explicit ban and extended enforcement tools raise litigation exposure for companies whose employees trade on inside knowledge.

analysis.trajectory: With introduction so late in the session, four cosponsors all from the minority party, and no committee action in the record, the bill is very unlikely to advance before the Congress ends on January 3, 2027; absent Banking Committee action, it will die at adjournment.
